notes: School bullying preliminary issues; Bradford-Smart duty analysis and dismissal are comprehensive.

enrichment.short_title: Shaw v Redbridge: school duty after playground harassment incident
key_facts: Natalie Shaw, a 13-year-old pupil at Valentines High School, alleged indecent assault and bullying by five boys on 13 October 1995.
Head of Year Mr Thompson investigated, punished the boys with short suspensions and lines, and advised her to tell her parents but did not contact them directly.
Ms Shaw later suffered serious psychiatric illness; she sued Redbridge LBC for negligence nearly ten years after the incident.
Preliminary issues were tried on existence, nature and extent of any duty of care and whether it was breached.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Trial of preliminary issues on duty of care and breach in negligence claim against education authority.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; no breach of duty found in failing to contact parents, refer for counselling or supervise pupils outside the head of year's office.
enrichment.ratio: Following Bradford-Smart, a school owes a duty to take such steps as a reasonable body of professional opinion would regard as appropriate; where an incident was reported as rough horseplay rather than indecent assault, a head of year could reasonably advise the pupil to tell her parents without directly contacting them, and causation of later psychiatric injury was not established on these issues.
legal_issues: Whether the school owed a duty of care for playground harassment reported to staff
Whether failure to contact parents directly was negligent
Whether the incident as reported warranted referral for counselling
Application of Bradford-Smart to bullying and school discipline
linked_authorities: Bradford-Smart v West Sussex County Council [2002] EWCA Civ 07
Hatton v Sutherland [2002] ICR 613
Barber v Somerset County Council [2004] ICR 457

confidence.notes: Preliminary issue findings and dismissal are clearly reasoned though causation and damage were reserved.

notes: Benefit fraud stay of proceedings; Walker J reversed magistrates on abuse of process standard.

enrichment.short_title: Herefordshire v Wiles: abuse of process stay for late CPIA disclosure
key_facts: Amanda Wiles faced magistrates' court charges of failing to notify a change in circumstances affecting housing and council tax benefit.
Defence solicitors requested disclosure including records of a telephone call and electronic files; prosecution disclosure was completed only on 10 June 2004, days before trial.
Magistrates stayed proceedings as an abuse of process because of alleged prejudice from delayed disclosure.
Herefordshire District Council appealed by case stated.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court appeal by case stated from magistrates' decision to stay criminal proceedings as abuse of process.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; magistrates' stay was not open to them in law; decision reversed and case remitted to a differently constituted bench.
enrichment.ratio: A stay for abuse of process on prejudice to defence requires serious prejudice such that no fair trial can be held; late disclosure shortly before trial can normally be addressed by adjournment under AG's Reference (No 1 of 1990), and magistrates must apply that test rather than treating incomplete disclosure alone as unjustifiable delay.
legal_issues: Whether failure to complete CPIA disclosure amounted to abuse of process
Whether prejudice to defence preparation was so serious that no fair trial was possible
Application of R v Derby Justices ex p Brooks and AG's Reference (No 1 of 1990)
Whether magistrates could stay on sense of justice grounds
linked_authorities: R v Derby Justices ex parte Brooks [1985] Cr App R 164
Attorney General's Reference (No 1 of 1990) [1992] QB 630
Bennett v Horseferry Road Magistrates' Court [1994] AC 42

confidence.notes: Answers to case stated questions and reversal are explicit.

notes: Time charter hull fouling arbitration appeal; Aikens J dismissed both implied indemnity and off-hire points.

enrichment.short_title: Action Navigation v Bottiglieri: hull fouling and off-hire on time charter
key_facts: Owners chartered the vessel Kitsa to Bottiglieri on amended NYPE terms within Institute Warranty Limits.
The vessel suffered hull fouling during prolonged discharge at Visakhapatnam, India, and Owners de-fouled at Portland at cost of about US$180,000.
Owners claimed implied indemnity for de-fouling costs and unpaid hire during cleaning; arbitrators rejected both claims.
Owners appealed with leave on scope of implied indemnity and application of clause 15 off-hire provision.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Commercial Court appeal with permission from arbitration award on time charterparty disputes.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed on both points; arbitrators' rejection of implied indemnity and off-hire award upheld.
enrichment.ratio: Where hull fouling from prolonged inactivity at a warm-water port was foreseeable when the charter was made, de-fouling expense is an ordinary trading risk borne by owners and outside an implied indemnity for lawful employment orders; off-hire during Portland cleaning fell under clause 54 for owners' purposes, not clause 15, following The Rijn.
legal_issues: Whether de-fouling costs were within implied indemnity for lawful port orders
Whether foreseeable fouling risk was agreed by owners at charter inception
Whether vessel was off-hire under clause 15 or clause 54 during de-fouling
Application of The Island Archon and The Rijn
linked_authorities: The Island Archon [1994] 2 Lloyd's Rep 227
Santa Martha Baay Scheepvaart v Scanbulk A/S (The Rijn) [1981] 2 Lloyd's Rep 267
Actis Co Ltd v The Sanko Steamship Co Ltd (The Aquacharm) [1980] 2 Lloyd's Rep 237

confidence.notes: Detailed reasoning on indemnity and off-hire though arbitrators' reasons were somewhat laconic.

notes: Oakley registered design validity preliminary issue; Prescott QC on ECA 1972 powers and Directive derogation timing.

enrichment.short_title: Oakley v Animal: registered design validity and ECA section 2(2) powers
key_facts: Oakley sued Animal for infringing its registered sunglasses design; Animal argued the registration was invalid for prior publication in May 1996.
The Designs Directive required transposition by 28 October 2001 but UK regulations implementing it, including a derogation preserving old validity rules, came into force on 9 December 2001.
A preliminary issue asked whether prior publication invalidated the design under old or new law and whether Regulation 12 was validly made.
The case raised constitutional questions about the scope of ministerial powers under section 2(2) of the 1972 Act.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Trial of preliminary issue of law on validity of registered design and vires of implementing regulations.
enrichment.outcome: Preliminary issue decided in favour of Animal; Regulation 12 severed to use 28 October 2001 cut-off date; possible ECJ reference on late derogation left open.
enrichment.ratio: A derogation under Article 11.8 of the Designs Directive could not extend validity rules to designs registered after the transposition deadline; late implementation catching post-deadline designs breached Community law, but Regulation 12 could be notionally revised to the mandated date under substantial severability, though whether the derogation option survived after the deadline may require ECJ clarification following Markopoulos.
legal_issues: Whether Oakley's 1996 publication invalidated registration under old or new validity rules
Limits of section 2(2) ECA powers to implement EU directives
Whether late transposition could lawfully exercise Article 11.8 derogation
Severability of Regulation 12 under DPP v Hutchinson
linked_authorities: Commission of the European Communities v Greece (Case C-294/01 Markopoulos)
DPP v Hutchinson [1990] 2 AC 783
Oakley Inc v Animal Ltd [2004] EWHC 3126 (Ch)

confidence.notes: Complex EU and constitutional analysis with one point reserved for possible ECJ reference.

notes: Blind software developer DDA appeal; Court of Appeal restored tribunal on justification test.

enrichment.short_title: Williams v JWT: disability discrimination against blind IT developer
key_facts: Sue Williams, totally blind, was employed by JWT as a Worldwide IT Developer despite lacking Lotus Notes experience.
JWT was ill prepared; essential JAWS screen-reader equipment arrived months late and she received little work or training for over a year.
The employment tribunal found unlawful discrimination and constructive unfair dismissal; the EAT remitted on justification.
JWT knew adjustments would be needed but failed adequately to investigate training costs and software adaptation.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal appeal from Employment Appeal Tribunal remittal in disability discrimination and constructive dismissal claim.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; original tribunal decision restored; constructive unfair dismissal held to be further act of disability discrimination.
enrichment.ratio: Where an employer knowingly hires a disabled employee for a role requiring training and equipment it has not provided, failure to investigate reasonable adjustments cannot be justified as material and substantial; the EAT improperly substituted its view for the tribunal's application of the Jones band-of-reasonable-responses test, and constructive dismissal may constitute discriminatory dismissal under section 4(2)(d) following Meikle.
legal_issues: Justification of less favourable treatment under section 5(3) DDA 1995
Duty to make reasonable adjustments under section 6
Whether EAT substituted its view on materiality and substantiality
Whether constructive dismissal was act of disability discrimination
linked_authorities: Jones v Post Office [2001] IRLR 634
Nottingham City Council v Meikle [2004] IRLR 703
Collins v Royal National Theatre Board Ltd [2004] IRLR 395
Archibald v Fife Council [2004] IRLR 651

confidence.notes: Appellate restoration of tribunal and Meikle constructive dismissal point are clearly reasoned.

notes: TA Major pension judicial review; Moses J held Directive directly effective but Regulation 13(2) compatible.

enrichment.short_title: Manson v MOD: part-time workers Regulations and Territorial Army pension

statutes_considered.title: Part-time Workers (Prevention of Less Favourable Treatment) Regulations 2000

key_facts: Major Manson, a long-serving Territorial Army officer, was denied a service pension for part-time reserve service.
His employment tribunal claim under the Part-time Workers Regulations failed; he challenged Regulation 13(2) excluding reserve training service.
He argued the Framework Agreement on part-time work required equal pension treatment and that TA service was not casual.
Judicial review was brought on compatibility of the exclusion with the Directive before EAT appeal was heard.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of compatibility of Part-time Workers Regulations exclusion for reserve forces with EU Framework Agreement.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; court lacked jurisdiction on private law right but held Directive directly effective and Regulation 13(2) compatible with casual part-time service exception.
enrichment.ratio: Members of the Territorial Army undertaking flexible training days perform casual part-time service within clause 2(2) of the Framework Agreement; excluding such service from pension parity under Regulation 13(2) is objectively justified by disproportionate administrative cost for short, low-volume reserve careers, and the pension claim remains a private law matter for employment tribunals.
legal_issues: Whether judicial review lay against denial of TA pension rights
Direct effect of Framework Agreement clause 4
Whether TA training service was casual part-time work
Objective justification for excluding reservists from Regulations
linked_authorities: Carmichael v National Power Plc [1999] ICR 1226
Cheng Yuen v Royal Hong Kong Golf Club [1998] ICR 131
Commission v Italy [1992] ECR I-3515

confidence.notes: Three-part conclusion on jurisdiction, direct effect and compatibility is explicit.

notes: Squatters JR on Pepys Estate; Collins J set aside permission and gave procedural guidance.

enrichment.short_title: Karkut v Lewisham: squatters and urgent judicial review procedure
key_facts: Squatters occupied vacant flats on Lewisham's Pepys Estate earmarked for demolition and redevelopment.
The council wrote demanding vacation and later brought county court possession proceedings.
Claimants sought judicial review via urgent N463 application; Henriques J granted permission and stayed proceedings.
Lewisham applied to set aside permission, arguing squatters had no Article 8 home right and council action was proportionate.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application to set aside grant of permission on urgent judicial review challenging possession proceedings against estate squatters.
enrichment.outcome: Permission set aside; claim held unarguable; squatters had no proportionate Article 8 defence; procedural guidance given on urgent JR applications.
enrichment.ratio: Granting permission on an urgent N463 application alongside interim relief is rarely appropriate when an interim order suffices; squatters with no lawful right to occupy cannot establish disproportionate eviction under Article 8, and a warning letter inviting contact is sufficient public law compliance before possession proceedings.
legal_issues: Whether council decision to sue squatters was amenable to judicial review
Article 8 home rights for unlawful squatters
Proportionality of possession against estate redevelopment squatters
Whether permission should be granted on urgent N463 applications
linked_authorities: Webb v Bristol City Council [2001] EWHC Civ 696
Turner J in Webb on inherent power to set aside permission

confidence.notes: Substantive dismissal and lead-judge procedural guidance are clearly expressed.

notes: Schedule 22 mandatory life tariff redetermination; 17-year minimum term confirmed.

enrichment.short_title: R v X: Schedule 22 mandatory life sentence minimum term determination
key_facts: XY was convicted of murder in 1998 for shooting his ex-wife's boyfriend ZW with a sawn-off shotgun during a violent confrontation at the former matrimonial home.
The trial judge and Lord Chief Justice recommended 17-18 years; the Home Secretary set a 17-year tariff before Anderson transferred tariff fixing to the judiciary.
XY applied under Schedule 22 of the 2003 Act for judicial redetermination of the minimum term.
He had previously given substantial assistance to law enforcement, which he argued should reduce the tariff.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court determination of minimum term under Schedule 22 Criminal Justice Act 2003 for existing mandatory life prisoner.
enrichment.outcome: Minimum term confirmed at 17 years less 4 days remand, applying Schedule 21 seriousness principles; prior police assistance did not reduce tariff.
enrichment.ratio: On Schedule 22 redetermination the court conducts a sentencing exercise applying Schedule 21 starting points and aggravating factors; substantial pre-offence assistance to police does not justify a lower murder tariff though it may affect later parole, and the court need not simply adopt prior judicial recommendations.
legal_issues: Appropriate minimum term under Schedule 21 for firearm murder
Whether pre-offence police assistance mitigates murder tariff
Interaction of prior Home Secretary tariff with Schedule 22 exercise
Application of Anderson sentencing principles
linked_authorities: R (Anderson) v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2002] UKHL 46
R v Riaz [2004] EWHC 74 (QB)
Practice Direction (Crime: Mandatory Life Sentences) (No. 2) [2002] 1 WLR 2551

confidence.notes: Tariff determination and reasoning on assistance are clearly stated.

notes: Hatton murder appeal; leave granted to revisit O'Grady intoxicated self-defence rule.

enrichment.short_title: Hatton: leave to appeal on intoxicated mistaken self-defence
key_facts: Jonathan Hatton killed Stuart Pashley with a sledgehammer in his flat after a night of heavy drinking.
He claimed vague recollection of being attacked with a sword-stick fashioned by himself; pathologist evidence showed savage multiple wounds.
The judge left self-defence to the jury but ruled that mistaken belief induced by voluntary intoxication could not support the defence, following R v O'Grady.
Hatton was convicted of murder in November 2003 at Sheffield Crown Court.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal application for leave to appeal against murder conviction on self-defence direction.
enrichment.outcome: Leave to appeal granted on whether O'Grady/O'Connor should be revisited for mistaken self-defence caused by voluntary intoxication.
enrichment.ratio: Where academic criticism of R v O'Grady warrants full argument and the judge left self-defence to the jury, the court may grant leave to reconsider whether a mistaken belief of necessity induced by voluntary intoxication can form part of a self-defence defence, notwithstanding the severity of the attack.
legal_issues: Whether voluntary intoxication can support mistaken self-defence belief
Binding effect of R v O'Grady and R v O'Connor
Whether sufficient evidence supported leaving self-defence
Proportionality of force when intoxicated
linked_authorities: R v O'Grady [1983] QB 1073
R v O'Connor [1991] Crim LR 135
R v Leten [1994] Crim LR 801

confidence.notes: Interlocutory leave judgment; merits of O'Grady challenge not finally decided.

notes: Morgan Est limitation joinder appeal; Jacob LJ on CPR 19.5 and Sardinia Sulcis test.

enrichment.short_title: Morgan Est v Hanson: mistaken claimant and CPR 19.5 substitution
key_facts: Miller Civil Engineering Ltd (company A) suffered damage from allegedly defective concrete pipes supplied by Hanson during tunnel construction.
Proceedings were issued against the limitation deadline naming Morgan Est Scotland Ltd (company B) as claimant, wrongly asserting it was the contracting purchaser.
Company A had assigned the cause of action to B, then B to Morgan Est plc (company C); solicitors sought to add A and C and substitute parties.
Hanson argued the amendment was outside CPR 19.5 and time-barred against the true contracting party.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal appeal from permission to amend claim by adding and substituting claimants after expiry of limitation period.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; substitution of A for B and joinder of C permitted under CPR 19.5; Sardinia Sulcis wrong-name test not the limit of the rule.
enrichment.ratio: CPR 19.5 implementing section 35 of the Limitation Act permits substitution where a party was named in mistake for the intending claimant without restricting the rule to the Sardinia Sulcis right-description-wrong-name test; the overriding objective supports correcting solicitor blunders that do not prejudice defendants.
legal_issues: Whether CPR 19.5 allowed substitution after limitation expired
Scope of mistake for substitution under rule 19.5
Whether Sardinia Sulcis test limits rule 19.5
Joinder of beneficial owner of assigned cause of action
linked_authorities: Evans v Charrington & Co Ltd [1984] 1 WLR 1157
Gregson v HAE [2003] EWCA Civ 1071
Three Rivers DC v Bank of England [1996] QB 292

confidence.notes: Appellate reasoning on CPR 19.5 scope and dismissal are comprehensive.
